text:
Recycling is widely encouraged, yet people disagree about whether it is mainly a personal duty or something that society and governments should organise. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual responsibility argue that everyday personal choices add up to a large environmental effect. Households decide whether to sort glass, paper and plastic or to throw everything into one bin, and careless sorting can spoil whole loads of recyclable material. Shoppers who choose products with less packaging also push companies to reduce waste. Without changed habits, even strong laws are hard to enforce. A family that separates its rubbish carefully every week, for example, keeps a large amount of material out of landfill, and a street where everyone does the same can cut its waste dramatically.

On the other hand, advocates of collective action point out that individuals alone cannot recycle what the system cannot process. A household cannot build a sorting plant or create a market for recycled materials, and many people live in areas where collection is irregular or unavailable. Governments can set rules that apply to everyone, such as deposit schemes and requirements for manufacturers to use recycled content, and only they can build the infrastructure that makes recycling practical. A resident with no collection point nearby, for instance, has little chance of recycling even when they want to.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that the most effective approach combines official leadership with personal action, since government provides the system and citizens supply the daily effort that makes it work.
